splits.legalQuestion: Whether a multiemployer pension plan actuary may select actuarial assumptions for calculating withdrawal liability after the statutory measurement date (the end of the prior plan year), or whether all such assumptions must be fixed by that date.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether ERISA's statutory measurement date for withdrawal liability requires all actuarial assumptions to be locked in by the end of the prior plan year, or whether actuaries may select assumptions after that date. This affects billions of dollars in potential obligations for employers participating in multiemployer pension plans.

positions.label: Assumptions must be fixed by measurement date
positions.summary: Holds that all actuarial assumptions must be determined as of the statutory measurement date (end of the prior plan year), providing employers with greater predictability about potential liability.

circuits.name: Seventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: M & K Employee Solutions v. Trustees of the IAM National Pension Fund

positions.label: Assumptions may be selected after measurement date
positions.summary: Holds that an actuary may select actuarial assumptions after the statutory measurement date, as the statute does not require all assumptions to be fixed by that date.

circuits.name: D.C. Circuit
circuits.caseName: M & K Employee Solutions v. Trustees of the IAM National Pension Fund

splits.relatedScotusTitle: M & K Employee Solutions v. Trustees of the IAM National Pension Fund

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the term of supervised release is tolled (paused) when a supervisee absconds from supervision, thereby extending the period during which the person can be found to have violated the conditions of supervised release.
splits.description: Circuits split on whether federal courts may apply a judicially-created 'fugitive tolling' doctrine to supervised release, effectively extending the period of court-ordered conditions beyond the time specified in the judgment when a person absconds. This affects thousands of individuals who abscond from supervised release each year.

positions.label: Supervised release is tolled during absconding
positions.summary: Holds that the term of supervised release is tolled when a supervisee absconds, extending the court's authority to revoke supervised release beyond the original expiration date.

positions.label: Supervised release is not tolled
positions.summary: Holds that there is no statutory or inherent authority to toll the term of supervised release when a supervisee absconds, as the statute does not provide for such tolling.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 2244(b)(1)'s bar on relitigating previously raised claims in habeas proceedings applies to federal prisoners filing motions under Section 2255.
splits.description: Circuits are split 6-to-3 on whether federal prisoners face the additional gatekeeping requirement of § 2244(b)(1) — which categorically bars raising any previously presented claim — when bringing successive collateral attacks under § 2255. If (b)(1) applies, federal prisoners face a stricter bar than Congress may have intended.

positions.label: Section 2244(b)(1) applies to § 2255 motions
positions.summary: Holds that § 2244(b)(1)'s categorical bar on previously raised claims applies to federal prisoners filing successive § 2255 motions, in addition to § 2255(h)'s own requirements.

positions.label: Section 2244(b)(1) does not apply to § 2255 motions
positions.summary: Holds that § 2244(b)(1)'s bar does not apply to federal prisoners filing under § 2255, so they need only satisfy § 2255(h)'s requirements of newly discovered evidence or a new rule of constitutional law.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a candidate for federal office has Article III standing to challenge a state law that allows the counting of mail-in ballots received after Election Day.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on the standards for evaluating whether candidates have standing to bring pre-election challenges to voting procedures. The resolution affects whether candidates can challenge mail-in voting rules, ballot counting deadlines, and other election administration practices before an election takes place.

positions.label: Candidates have standing
positions.summary: Holds that candidates suffer a cognizable injury from election rules that allegedly dilute lawful votes or change the competitive landscape, granting them standing to challenge such laws pre-election.

positions.label: Candidates lack standing
positions.summary: Holds that a candidate's alleged competitive injury from a state election law is too speculative or generalized to establish Article III standing, particularly for pre-election challenges.

circuits.name: Seventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: Bost v. Illinois State Board of Elections

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Bost v. Illinois State Board of Elections

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the rule of lenity takes priority over deference to agency interpretations (Auer/Kisor deference) when interpreting ambiguous provisions in the Sentencing Guidelines that increase criminal penalties.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether courts should defer to the Sentencing Commission's anti-defendant interpretation of ambiguous Guidelines provisions or instead apply the rule of lenity in favor of the defendant. This split has deepened after Loper Bright Enterprises v. Raimondo overruled Chevron deference.

positions.label: Lenity trumps deference
positions.summary: Holds that the rule of lenity should prevail over agency deference when interpreting ambiguous criminal sentencing provisions, preventing agencies from expanding criminal liability without explicit statutory authorization.

positions.label: Deference trumps lenity
positions.summary: Holds that agency deference (Auer/Kisor deference to the Sentencing Commission's commentary) takes priority over the rule of lenity when interpreting ambiguous Guidelines provisions, even in criminal sentencing contexts.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the word 'and' in the First Step Act's safety-valve provision, 18 U.S.C. § 3553(f)(1), is conjunctive (requiring all three criminal-history criteria to be met for disqualification) or disjunctive (any one criterion is disqualifying).
splits.description: Circuits are deeply split on whether 'and' means 'and' or 'or' in the safety-valve provision, which governs whether district courts must impose sentences without regard to statutory minimums. The split leads to dramatically different sentences for defendants with identical criminal histories depending on the circuit.

positions.label: 'And' is conjunctive — all three criteria required
positions.summary: Holds that defendants are disqualified from safety-valve relief only if they meet all three criminal-history criteria listed in § 3553(f)(1), reading 'and' as conjunctive.

positions.label: 'And' is disjunctive — any one criterion disqualifies
positions.summary: Holds that possessing any one of the three criminal-history criteria disqualifies a defendant from safety-valve relief, reading 'and' as disjunctive or distributive.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Application Note 1 to U.S.S.G. § 4B1.2, which includes inchoate offenses like conspiracy in the definition of 'controlled substance offense,' is entitled to deference when the guideline text does not mention such offenses.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether the Sentencing Commission's commentary can expand the definition of 'controlled substance offense' to include conspiracy and other inchoate offenses not mentioned in the guideline text, particularly after Kisor v. Wilkie narrowed deference to agency interpretations of their own regulations.

positions.label: Commentary is authoritative and includes inchoate offenses
positions.summary: Holds that Application Note 1 is an authoritative interpretation of the career-offender guideline entitled to deference under Stinson, and thus conspiracy qualifies as a controlled substance offense for career-offender purposes.

positions.label: Guideline text is unambiguous and excludes inchoate offenses
positions.summary: Holds that the text of § 4B1.2(b) unambiguously does not include inchoate offenses, and Application Note 1 impermissibly expands the guideline beyond its text, so conspiracy does not qualify as a predicate.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a state drug conviction qualifies as a 'controlled substance offense' under the Sentencing Guidelines when the state-law substance is not controlled under the federal Controlled Substances Act.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether the Guidelines' definition of 'controlled substance offense' requires the underlying substance to be federally scheduled or whether a state conviction for any substance controlled under state law suffices. This affects career-offender and other sentencing enhancements.

positions.label: State schedule controls — no federal match required
positions.summary: Holds that the Guidelines broadly define 'controlled substance offense' to include offenses under state law, without requiring the substance to be federally scheduled.

positions.label: Federal schedule controls — substance must be federally listed
positions.summary: Holds that a state drug conviction qualifies as a controlled substance offense under the Guidelines only if the substance is also controlled under the federal Controlled Substances Act.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a district court may expressly base a revocation sentence on the need to punish the defendant for violating conditions of supervised release, or whether revocation sentences must be based solely on the breach of trust and the statutory factors in 18 U.S.C. § 3583(e).
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether district courts may impose revocation sentences that expressly punish defendants for their violation conduct. The Sixth Circuit allows explicit punishment rationales, placing it at the extreme of a circuit split, while other circuits limit revocation sentences to addressing the breach of the court's trust.

positions.label: Punishment is permissible at revocation
positions.summary: Holds that district courts may expressly punish defendants for violations of supervised release conditions when revoking supervision and imposing a new term of imprisonment.

positions.label: Punishment is not the purpose of revocation
positions.summary: Holds that revocation sentences should be based on the defendant's breach of trust with the court and the statutory factors, not on punishing the defendant for the underlying violation conduct.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the First Step Act's non-retroactive anti-stacking amendment to 18 U.S.C. § 924(c) can constitute an 'extraordinary and compelling reason' for compassionate release under 18 U.S.C. § 3582(c)(1)(A), and whether the Sentencing Commission's 2024 policy statement (U.S.S.G. § 1B1.13(b)(6)) permitting such consideration exceeds the Commission's authority.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether non-retroactive changes in sentencing law, such as the First Step Act's elimination of mandatory stacking for § 924(c) convictions, can be considered as extraordinary and compelling reasons for compassionate release. The Seventh Circuit holds that they cannot and that the Commission exceeded its authority in saying otherwise, while other circuits have permitted such consideration.

positions.label: Non-retroactive changes cannot support compassionate release
positions.summary: Holds that a non-retroactive change in law cannot contribute to a finding of extraordinary and compelling reasons for sentence reduction, and the Sentencing Commission's policy statement to the contrary exceeds its statutory authority.

positions.label: Non-retroactive changes may support compassionate release
positions.summary: Holds that non-retroactive changes in sentencing law may be considered, alone or in combination with other factors, as extraordinary and compelling reasons warranting a sentence reduction under § 3582(c)(1)(A).

splits.legalQuestion: Whether federal prisoners challenging conditions or terms of confinement (as opposed to the fact or duration of confinement) must proceed through habeas corpus or may bring claims under Bivens or other civil rights statutes.
splits.description: A longstanding circuit split exists on whether habeas corpus is the exclusive federal remedy for all challenges to confinement, including conditions and terms, or whether non-habeas civil rights actions remain available for challenges that do not directly contest the fact or duration of imprisonment. This affects federal prisoners' ability to challenge BOP decisions on prerelease custody, earned time credits, and other conditions.

positions.label: Habeas is exclusive for challenges affecting duration
positions.summary: Holds that challenges to BOP decisions affecting the duration or execution of confinement, including prerelease custody decisions, must be brought through habeas corpus and not civil rights actions.

positions.label: Civil rights actions available for conditions challenges
positions.summary: Holds that challenges to conditions or terms of confinement that do not seek immediate or speedier release may proceed through civil rights actions rather than habeas corpus.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a motion for attorney's fees under the Hyde Amendment in a criminal case is subject to the civil appeal deadline (30 days) or the criminal appeal deadline (14 days).
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether a Hyde Amendment motion — which allows criminal defendants to recoup fees from frivolous, vexatious, or bad-faith prosecutions — is a civil matter ancillary to the criminal case (triggering the 30-day deadline) or part of the criminal proceeding (triggering the 14-day deadline).

positions.label: Civil deadline applies
positions.summary: Holds that a Hyde Amendment motion for attorney's fees is a civil matter ancillary to the criminal case, subject to the 30-day civil appeal deadline under Federal Rule of Appellate Procedure 4(a).

positions.label: Criminal deadline applies
positions.summary: Holds that a Hyde Amendment motion is part of the criminal case and subject to the 14-day criminal appeal deadline under Federal Rule of Appellate Procedure 4(b).

splits.legalQuestion: Whether post-petition, pre-conversion increases in the equity of an asset belong to the bankruptcy estate or to debtors who convert in good faith from Chapter 13 to Chapter 7 under 11 U.S.C. § 348(f)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether property appreciation occurring between a Chapter 13 filing and a good-faith conversion to Chapter 7 inures to the bankruptcy estate or remains with the debtor. The Ninth Circuit holds it belongs to the estate, creating a split with other circuits that hold it belongs to the debtor.

positions.label: Appreciation belongs to the estate
positions.summary: Holds that post-petition, pre-conversion appreciation in property value belongs to the bankruptcy estate upon conversion, based on the broad scope of § 541(a)'s definition of estate property.

positions.label: Appreciation belongs to the debtor
positions.summary: Holds that under § 348(f)(1)(A), post-petition, pre-conversion appreciation belongs to the debtor in a good-faith conversion, consistent with the statute's structure, purpose, and legislative history.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether an order denying a motion to seal documents containing private medical information is immediately appealable under the collateral order doctrine.
splits.description: Circuits take different approaches to whether denial of a motion to seal medical records qualifies as an immediately appealable collateral order. The D.C. Circuit held such orders are appealable because medical privacy is a value of 'high order,' while other circuits have been more restrictive about extending the collateral order doctrine to sealing denials.

positions.label: Immediately appealable
positions.summary: Holds that denying a motion to seal medical records is immediately appealable under the collateral order doctrine because maintaining privacy in medical treatments and diagnoses is a value of high order that would be irreparably lost absent immediate review.

positions.label: Not immediately appealable
positions.summary: Holds that orders denying motions to seal generally do not satisfy the collateral order doctrine's requirements because there are adequate alternative means to protect privacy interests, such as protective orders.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Religious Land Use and Institutionalized Persons Act (RLUIPA) authorizes individual-capacity damages suits against state prison officials, and whether Congress has constitutional power under the Spending Clause to impose such personal liability.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether RLUIPA permits suits for money damages against prison officials in their individual capacities. Some circuits allow such suits while others hold that RLUIPA does not clearly authorize individual-capacity damages, raising questions about the scope of Congressional spending power to impose personal liability on non-recipients of federal funds.

positions.label: RLUIPA allows individual-capacity damages
positions.summary: Holds that RLUIPA authorizes suits for money damages against state prison officials in their individual capacities, as the statute's text is broad enough to encompass such claims.

circuits.name: Fifth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Landor v. Louisiana Dep't of Corrections

positions.label: RLUIPA does not authorize individual-capacity damages
positions.summary: Holds that RLUIPA does not clearly authorize individual-capacity damages suits against state prison officials, and Spending Clause legislation cannot impose personal liability on individuals who are not direct recipients of federal funds.

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Landor v. Louisiana Department of Corrections and Public Safety

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a district court may consider factors related to potential errors or unfairness in a defendant's conviction or sentence as part of the 'extraordinary and compelling reasons' analysis for compassionate release under 18 U.S.C. § 3582(c)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether compassionate release motions may be used to raise claims that overlap with habeas corpus challenges, such as alleged sentencing errors or constitutional violations in the underlying conviction. Some circuits permit consideration of such factors, while others hold that § 3582(c)(1)(A) cannot be used as a substitute for § 2255 habeas relief.

positions.label: May consider conviction/sentence errors
positions.summary: Holds that district courts may consider legal errors or unfairness in a defendant's conviction or sentence as one factor in the extraordinary and compelling reasons analysis for compassionate release.

positions.label: Cannot use compassionate release for habeas-type claims
positions.summary: Holds that § 3582(c)(1)(A) is not an alternative avenue for claims properly raised under § 2255, and errors in conviction or sentencing cannot constitute extraordinary and compelling reasons for compassionate release.

splits.legalQuestion: What legal standards govern claims of discrimination or unfair treatment in the operation of hospitality or business establishments under federal civil rights law?
splits.description: The Supreme Court granted certiorari to resolve disagreement among circuits over the standards for discrimination claims against hospitality and business operators, including questions about liability and available remedies. The Second Circuit's approach was deemed sufficiently unsettled to warrant review.

positions.label: Broader liability standards
positions.summary: Holds that broader standards apply to discrimination claims against business establishments, potentially allowing for more expansive remedies.

positions.label: Narrower liability standards
positions.summary: Holds that narrower standards govern such claims, limiting the scope of liability and available remedies for discrimination in public accommodations.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Aviation Administration Authorization Act of 1994 (FAAAA) preempts state-law negligence claims against freight brokers who arrange transportation of property by motor carriers.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether the FAAAA's broad preemption clause, which prohibits states from enacting laws 'related to a price, route, or service of any... broker,' preempts common-law negligence claims against freight brokers for injuries arising from the carrier's operations. This split affects the liability exposure of freight brokers nationwide.

positions.label: FAAAA preempts broker negligence claims
positions.summary: Holds that state-law negligence claims against freight brokers are preempted by the FAAAA because they relate to the broker's services in arranging transportation.

circuits.name: Ninth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Miller v. C.H. Robinson Worldwide, Inc.

positions.label: FAAAA does not preempt broker negligence claims
positions.summary: Holds that state-law negligence claims against freight brokers are not preempted by the FAAAA because they are generally applicable common-law duties rather than regulations targeting broker services.

circuits.name: Eleventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: Montgomery v. Caribe Transport II, LLC

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Montgomery v. Caribe Transport II, LLC

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Insecticide, Fungicide, and Rodenticide Act (FIFRA) preempts state-law failure-to-warn claims based on allegedly inadequate product labeling when the EPA has not required the specific warning.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether FIFRA's preemption provision bars state-law failure-to-warn claims against pesticide manufacturers when the claim is based on the absence of a warning that the EPA did not require. The split affects product liability litigation involving agricultural chemicals and consumer pesticide products.

positions.label: FIFRA preempts failure-to-warn claims
positions.summary: Holds that FIFRA preempts state-law failure-to-warn claims that would effectively require labeling different from or in addition to what FIFRA and EPA regulations permit.

positions.label: FIFRA does not preempt failure-to-warn claims
positions.summary: Holds that FIFRA does not preempt state-law failure-to-warn claims because such claims impose requirements 'parallel to' rather than 'in addition to' FIFRA's labeling requirements.

circuits.name: Third Circuit
circuits.caseName: DeKalb Genetics Corp. v. Bayer CropScience

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Monsanto Company v. John L. Durnell

splits.legalQuestion: Whether 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(3), which prohibits unlawful users of controlled substances from possessing firearms, violates the Second Amendment as applied to marijuana users.
splits.description: Following the Supreme Court's decision in Bruen, circuits have split on whether § 922(g)(3)'s prohibition on firearm possession by users of controlled substances — particularly marijuana — is constitutional. Some circuits have upheld the law under historical tradition analysis, while others have found it unconstitutional as applied to marijuana users.

positions.label: Section 922(g)(3) is constitutional
positions.summary: Holds that § 922(g)(3)'s prohibition on firearm possession by unlawful drug users is consistent with the nation's historical tradition of firearm regulation and survives Second Amendment scrutiny.

positions.label: Section 922(g)(3) is unconstitutional as applied
positions.summary: Holds that § 922(g)(3) violates the Second Amendment as applied to marijuana users because the government has not demonstrated a historical tradition of disarming persons who use intoxicating substances.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether workers who distribute baked goods to retail stores qualify as 'transportation workers engaged in foreign or interstate commerce' under Section 1 of the Federal Arbitration Act, thereby exempting them from mandatory arbitration agreements.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on the scope of the FAA's Section 1 transportation worker exemption, specifically whether workers who distribute goods to retail stores as part of a broader interstate distribution chain are 'transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce.' The split affects the enforceability of arbitration agreements for a broad class of last-mile delivery workers.

positions.label: Broad interpretation — last-mile workers exempt
positions.summary: Holds that workers who distribute goods to retail stores as part of an interstate distribution chain are transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce exempt from the FAA.

positions.label: Narrow interpretation — last-mile workers not exempt
positions.summary: Holds that workers who merely distribute goods locally to retail stores are not transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce and remain subject to FAA arbitration agreements.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 47(b) of the Investment Company Act creates a private right of action allowing parties to a contract that violates the ICA to sue in federal court for rescission of that contract.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether § 47(b) of the ICA provides an implied private right of action for rescission of contracts made in violation of the Act. This affects the ability of private parties to enforce the ICA's protections against abusive investment company practices through direct federal court actions.

positions.label: Section 47(b) creates a private right of action
positions.summary: Holds that § 47(b) creates an implied private right of action for rescission of contracts that violate the Investment Company Act, allowing private parties to sue directly.

circuits.name: Second Circuit
circuits.caseName: FS Credit Opportunities Corp. v. Saba Capital Master Fund

positions.label: Section 47(b) does not create a private right of action
positions.summary: Holds that § 47(b) is a voidability provision rather than a private right of action, and only the SEC can enforce the ICA's prohibitions.

splits.relatedScotusTitle: FS Credit Opportunities Corp. v. Saba Capital Master Fund

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act, as construed under the Gingles framework, can constitutionally compel race-based redistricting as a remedy for vote dilution, and whether compliance with Section 2 constitutes a compelling governmental interest justifying the use of race in drawing district lines.
splits.description: This case raises the question of whether race-conscious redistricting mandated by Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act is constitutionally permissible under the Equal Protection Clause. Lower courts have applied the Gingles framework to require consideration of race, but the constitutionality of this framework as applied is increasingly contested.

positions.label: Section 2 compels constitutionally permissible race-conscious redistricting
positions.summary: Holds that compliance with Section 2 of the VRA, as interpreted under the Gingles framework, constitutes a compelling interest that justifies the use of race in drawing district lines.

positions.label: Section 2's compelled race-based redistricting raises constitutional concerns
positions.summary: Holds or suggests that the Gingles framework's requirement of race-based redistricting may exceed constitutional limits under the Equal Protection Clause, particularly after Dobbs-era equal protection jurisprudence.

circuits.name: Eighth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Arkansas State Conference of the NAACP v. Arkansas Board of Apportionment
